## Chapter 1

[Lucian]

I stand at the floor-to-ceiling windows of my penthouse office, gazing out at the city sprawled beneath me. The setting sun casts a golden glow across the skyline, turning the glass and steel of skyscrapers into a glittering tapestry. It's a view I never tire of—a constant reminder of the empire I've built and the power I wield.

My eyes narrow as I spot a sleek black car pulling up to the building. Right on time. I adjust my cufflinks, the cool metal a stark contrast to the heat simmering beneath my skin. The thrill of the impending meeting courses through my veins, a potent cocktail of anticipation and barely restrained aggression.

The intercom buzzes, and my assistant's voice filters through. "Mr. Kane, your guests have arrived."

"Send them up," I reply, my voice low and controlled.

I turn from the window, surveying my domain. The office is a testament to power and wealth—all dark wood, gleaming chrome, and leather; every item carefully chosen to intimidate and impress. I settle into the high-backed chair behind my imposing desk—a throne from which I rule my kingdom.

The door opens and three men enter. Their expensive suits and confident strides speak of wealth and influence, but I can smell the fear radiating off them. Good. They should be afraid.

"Gentlemen," I greet them, my voice a silky purr that belies the steel beneath. "Please, have a seat."

They arrange themselves in the chairs before my desk, their eyes darting nervously around the room. I let the silence stretch, enjoying their discomfort. Finally, the boldest of the three speaks up.

"Mr. Kane, we appreciate you taking the time to meet with us," he begins, his voice steady despite the sweat beading on his brow. "We believe this merger could be incredibly beneficial for both our companies."

I lean back in my chair, steepling my fingers. "Beneficial," I repeat, letting the word hang in the air. "An interesting choice of words. Tell me, Mr. Hanson, how exactly do you see this benefiting me?"

Hanson swallows hard, his Adam's apple bobbing. "Well, sir, with our resources combined, we could corner the market in—"

I cut him off with a sharp gesture. "I'm well aware of the potential market share. What I'm interested in is what you're willing to sacrifice to make this happen."

The men exchange uneasy glances. I can practically see the gears turning in their heads, weighing the risk against the potential reward. It's a game I've played countless times, and I always come out on top.

"Mr. Kane." The second man, Peterson, leans forward. "We're prepared to offer a significant portion of our holdings. Fifty-one percent, to be exact."

A smirk tugs at the corner of my mouth. "Fifty-one percent. How generous of you to offer me the bare minimum controlling interest."

Peterson blanches, realizing his misstep. "Of course, we're open to negotiation—"

"Seventy percent," I interrupt, my tone brooking no argument. "And full control of your overseas operations."

The third man, Roberts, sputters in disbelief. "But that's… that's practically everything!"

I fix him with a cold stare and he shrinks back in his seat. "It's everything, or it's nothing. Your choice, gentlemen."

The tension in the room is palpable as they huddle together, whispering furiously. I watch them with detached amusement, already knowing the outcome. They'll agree. They always do.

Finally, Hanson turns back to me, defeat written across his face. "We accept your terms, Mr. Kane."

I allow myself a small, victorious smile. "Excellent. My legal team will draw up the contracts. I expect them signed by tomorrow evening."

They nod, looking shell-shocked as they rise to leave. As they reach the door, I call out, "Oh, and gentlemen? I trust this goes without saying, but if I catch even a whisper of you trying to back out or renegotiate, the consequences will be... severe."

The threat hangs in the air, heavy and unmistakable. They hurry out, practically tripping over themselves in their haste to escape.

As the door closes behind them, I allow myself a moment of satisfaction. Another conquest, another piece added to my ever-expanding empire. But the feeling is fleeting, quickly replaced by the constant hunger for more.

A knock at the door interrupts my thoughts. "Enter," I call out.

Ryan Carter, my right-hand man and head of security, steps into the office. His face is impassive, but I can read the tension in the set of his shoulders.

"Report," I command, leaning back in my chair.

Ryan clears his throat. "Sir, we've encountered a... situation with the shipment from Colombia."

My eyes narrow dangerously. "Explain."

"One of our men got sloppy. Left a paper trail that could be traced back to us." Ryan's voice is carefully neutral, but I can hear the undercurrent of concern.

I feel a surge of cold anger. Sloppiness is unacceptable in my organization. "Who?"

"Jackson, sir. The new recruit."

I nod slowly, my mind already formulating a plan. "Bring him to me. Now."

Ryan hesitates for a moment. "Sir, perhaps we should consider—"

"Now, Ryan," I growl, my patience wearing thin.

He nods sharply and exits the office. I rise from my chair, moving to stand by the window once more. The city lights flicker to life as darkness falls, a stark reminder of the shadowy world I inhabit.

Minutes later, the door opens again. Ryan enters, followed by a young man who can't be more than twenty-five. Jackson, I presume. He's pale and visibly shaking, his eyes wide with terror.

"Mr. Kane, I-I'm so sorry," he stammers. "I didn't mean to—"

I hold up a hand, silencing him instantly. "Do you understand the gravity of your mistake, Jackson?"

He nods frantically. "Yes, sir. I swear it won't happen again."

"You're right," I say softly, dangerously. "It won't."

In one fluid motion, I close the distance between us. My hand shoots out, gripping his throat. I lift him off his feet, slamming him against the wall. His eyes bulge in terror as he gasps for air.

"Let me make something very clear," I hiss, my face inches from his. "Mistakes like this put everything I've built at risk. I don't tolerate risks."

I release him, and he crumples to the floor, coughing and sputtering. "Please," he wheezes. "I'll do anything. Just give me another chance."

I look down at him, contempt curling my lip. "You had your chance. You failed." I turn to Ryan. "Get him out of my sight. You know what to do."

Ryan nods grimly, hauling the sobbing man to his feet and dragging him from the office. As the door closes behind them, I straighten my tie, pushing down the simmering rage.

I've barely had a moment to collect myself when my phone rings. The caller ID shows an unlisted number—one I recognize all too well. I answer, my voice cool and controlled. "Speak."

The voice on the other end is terse, urgent. "We have a problem. There's a lawyer sniffing around the Westbrook deal. She's good, Kane. Too good."

I feel a flicker of irritation. The Westbrook deal is a crucial piece of my latest expansion. Any threat to it is unacceptable. "Who is she?"

"Name's Sophie Martin. Up-and-coming corporate attorney. Word is she's ruthless in the courtroom."

A smirk tugs at my lips. Ruthless. How intriguing. "Send me everything you have on her. I'll handle it personally."

I end the call, my mind already racing with possibilities. This Sophie Martin might prove to be a worthy adversary. The thought sends a thrill of excitement through me. It's been too long since I've had a real challenge.

I turn back to the window, gazing out at my city once more. In the reflection of the glass, I see my own wolfish smile. Let her come. I'll crush her like I've crushed everyone else who's dared to stand in my way.

## Chapter 2

[Sophie]

I push open the weathered door of Martin & Associates, the brass nameplate dulled by years of neglect. The familiar scent of old paper and coffee greets me, a bittersweet reminder of better days. Our once-bustling office now feels hollow, the empty desks like tombstones marking the graves of our former success.

Shrugging off my coat, I make my way to my cramped office, my heels clicking against the worn linoleum. The sound echoes in the quiet space, a stark contrast to the cacophony of ringing phones and bustling paralegals that used to fill these halls.

"Morning, Sophie," Marcus calls out as I pass his desk. "There's fresh coffee in the break room."

I nod gratefully, pausing at his desk. "Thanks, Marcus. Any messages?"

He hands me a small stack of pink slips. "Just these. Oh, and Lucy wants to see you when you have a moment. She seemed... excited about something."

Intrigued, I head to my office, dropping my bag on the cluttered desk before making my way to the break room. As I pour myself a cup of coffee, my mind races with possibilities. What could have Lucy so worked up?

Coffee in hand, I knock on Lucy's office door. "Come in!" her voice calls out, tinged with barely contained enthusiasm.

I enter to find my sister practically vibrating with energy, her eyes sparkling with a fierce determination I haven't seen in months. "Sophie," she says, gesturing for me to sit. "You're not going to believe what just landed in our laps."

Settling into the chair across from her desk, I raise an eyebrow. "Well, don't keep me in suspense. What's got you so fired up?"

Lucy leans forward, her voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper. "We've been approached about a potential case against Westbrook Industries."

I nearly choke on my coffee. "Westbrook? As in the multi-billion dollar conglomerate? Lucy, that's—"

"I know," she interrupts, her excitement palpable. "It's huge. And risky as hell. But Sophie, if we could pull this off..."

I set my mug down, my mind already racing with the implications. "It could save the firm," I finish for her. "But Lucy, we're talking about going up against one of the most powerful corporations in the country. They have armies of lawyers and bottomless pockets. We're... well, we're us."

Lucy's expression softens, a hint of vulnerability showing through her usual bravado. "I know it's a long shot, Soph. But what other choice do we have? We're barely keeping the lights on as it is."

She's right, and we both know it. The past year has been a slow, painful descent into financial ruin. We've lost clients, had to let go of staff, and the bills keep piling up. This case could be our salvation... or our final nail in the coffin.

"Tell me everything," I say, leaning forward.

For the next hour, Lucy briefs me on the case. It's a complex web of corporate espionage, insider trading, and environmental violations. The evidence is compelling, but circumstantial. It's going to be an uphill battle, to say the least.

As Lucy talks, I can feel a familiar fire igniting in my chest. This is why I became a lawyer—to fight for justice, to stand up to the powerful on behalf of the powerless. It's been too long since I've felt this spark.

"What do you think?" Lucy asks as she finishes her overview. "I know it's risky, but—"

I hold up a hand, cutting her off. "You're right. It is risky. But it's also exactly the kind of case we got into this business for."

A slow smile spreads across Lucy's face. "So, you're in?"

"I'm in," I confirm, feeling a surge of adrenaline at the decision. "But we need to be smart about this. We can't go in half-cocked."

Lucy nods, her expression turning serious. "Agreed. I've got the initial evidence files here. Why don't you take them and start reviewing? We can reconvene this afternoon to start strategizing."

I gather the files, the weight of them a physical reminder of the enormity of what we're undertaking. As I turn to leave, Lucy calls out, "Sophie?"

I pause at the door, looking back at my sister. Her face is a mix of hope and fear, mirroring my own conflicted emotions. "Be careful, okay? Westbrook... they play dirty. If we're going to do this, we need to be prepared for anything."

I nod, a grim determination settling over me. "Don't worry, Luce. I can handle myself."

Back in my office, I spread the files across my desk, losing myself in the intricacies of the case. Hours pass in a blur of financial reports, environmental impact studies, and witness statements. The more I read, the more certain I become that we're onto something big.

A soft knock at my door pulls me from my focus. I look up to see Marcus standing in the doorway, concern etched on his face. "Sophie, it's past seven. You should think about calling it a night."

I blink, surprised to see how dark it's gotten outside. "Thanks, Marcus. I just got caught up in..." I gesture vaguely at the mess of papers covering my desk.

He steps into the office, his eyes widening as he takes in the scope of what I'm working on. "Is this the Westbrook case Lucy mentioned?"

I nod, running a hand through my hair. "Yeah. It's... it's big, Marcus. Bigger than anything we've ever taken on."

Marcus perches on the edge of my desk. "Are you sure about this, Sophie?" he asks, his voice soft with concern. "Going up against Westbrook... it's not just David versus Goliath. It's David versus an entire army of Goliaths."

I lean back in my chair, meeting his worried gaze. "I know. But Marcus, if we can pull this off... it could change everything. Not just for the firm, but for all the people Westbrook has hurt."

He studies me for a long moment, then nods slowly. "Okay. If you're sure, then I'm with you. All the way."

The sincerity in his voice touches me, and I smile gratefully. "Thank you, Marcus. That means more than you know."

As Marcus leaves, I turn back to the files, losing myself once more in the intricacies of the case. Westbrook's transgressions go deeper than I could have imagined—a tangled web of corruption and greed that makes my blood boil.

As the night wears on, my determination only grows stronger. This case is more than just a lifeline for our struggling firm—it's a chance to make a real difference, to hold the powerful accountable for their actions.

Finally, as the first hints of dawn start to peek through my office window, I lean back in my chair, my mind made up. We're going to take this case, consequences be damned. Westbrook might have armies of lawyers and bottomless pockets, but we have the truth on our side. And I'll be damned if I let them get away with their crimes.

I gather the most damning pieces of evidence, arranging them carefully in a folder. Tomorrow—or rather, today—I'll present my findings to Lucy and we'll start planning our strategy. As I stand to leave, my eyes fall on a photo on my desk. It's of Lucy and me on the day we opened the firm, our faces beaming with hope and ambition.

"We're going to save this place," I whisper to the smiling faces in the photo. "No matter what it takes."

With a final glance at the mountain of evidence I've compiled, I make my way out of the office. The weight of what we're about to undertake settles on my shoulders, a mix of exhilaration and trepidation coursing through my veins.

As I step out into the cool morning air, I take a deep breath, steeling myself for the battle ahead. Westbrook won't know what hit them. Let them bring their armies of lawyers and bottomless pockets. I'm ready for war.

## Chapter 1

From the spotless black Bentley, I stepped out. The cool Manhattan night air brushed against me. The shimmering city skyline scoffed at my restlessness: Gone were the days when a night out to yet another high-society event demanded that I play the part of a perfect mafia princess. Something about the thought sent shivers down my spine.

My entrance into the Plaza Hotel ballroom initiated a spectacle with the gazes of a hundred onlookers being held, a sensation I had never experienced before. The glass chandeliers would bathe the scene in glorious radiance: the splendid backdrop of the sea with designer gowns and tailored suits showcased under an artist's hand, only I felt the warm rays meant to spotlight my every move. 

I scanned the room for some kind of acquaintance or a friend in that mass of Malice and Viciousness that New York City could muster. My eyes landed upon my cousin, Giordanna, and I walked over to her, hoping for a somewhat merciful reprieve from the stifling atmosphere in the place.

Having grown up witnessing this via her eyes, she was one among our cadre of old friends."Giordanna smiled mischievously: "Val, you look stunning. I was beginning to think you'd sneak out on us tonight."

I let out a weak smile while accepting a glass of bubbly from a passing waiter. "Trust me, that thought did occur to me again," I said, sipping while enjoying the bubbles bursting against my tongue. "I just don't know any other way to take this, Gia."

Giordanna's face softened, and her eyes filled with understanding. "Surely it isn't easy, but you know how much these events mean to Uncle Sal. To the family…"

"The family expects me to be here, I know," I interrupted, with bitterness in my voice. "The family expects me to smile, to charm, to be their perfect little pawn. When am I going to get to live for myself?"

Giordanna looked around nervously to make sure no one was within eavesdropping. "Val, be careful. You know how dangerous it is to even think about leaving."

I sighed and ran my hand through my carefully styled hair. "No, Gia, I'm not talking about leaving. I want more than this. More than being paraded around like a trophy, more than being married off as a broodmare to strengthen alliances. Is that too much to ask?"

Before Giordanna could respond, there was a loud noise near the entrance, and as the crowd began to pull away, I saw him.

He moved around the room like a predator; his presence was felt, and he commanded attention with each step. His dark eyes scanned the crowd, sharp and calculated, as if he were assessing every person in his way. He looked dangerous, like a man who could destroy anything or anyone that stood in his way. The perfectly tailored suit only enhanced the raw masculinity that seemed to radiate from him; at every point, he exuded authority and control.

"Who is that?" I breathed in a whisper, unable to stop staring, my pulse racing faster with every second he seemed to be moving nearer to me.

Giordanna followed my line of sight; her lips curled into a smile implying much. "That's Aldo Cavalli. He is new to town, just arrived from Chicago. Rumour has it that he intends to expand his business interests, but what exactly those are... well, that depends on who you ask."

Aldo was moved through the crowd. Exchanging pleasantries with a few men, whose names I barely registered. He was carrying himself with tremendous confidence while underneath, something dark. His smile has charm, but his eyes are empty. It's as though the predator is amusing itself by gently testing its prey. 

There was something that made my breath get caught in my throat, a danger I dreaded but was irrationally attracted to. My heart pounded as he drew near. For some reason, half of me wanted to see what would unfold between those eyes and me. 

Val, be careful; I am warning you, those men are nothing but trouble.

I turned to her, full of defiance. "Maybe what I need is trouble.

Before I could second-guess myself, I handed my empty glass to Giordanna and moved across the room. My heart pounded with each step, a strange mix of excitement and uncertainty. It felt as if I was walking straight into something dangerous. Still, there was something about him that drew me in, made me want to see just how close I could get before it all went wrong.

Aldo’s eyes found mine as I approached, and suddenly the entire room seemed to fall away, leaving just us. Up close, he was even more striking than I’d realized, with sharp features, a strong jaw, and those dark eyes that made it impossible to hide anything. There was more to him than just being attractive; he had a sense of danger that I couldn’t ignore, no matter how much I told myself to be careful.

“Mr. Cavalli,” I said, keeping my voice steady even as nerves raced through me. I held out my hand, aware of how close we stood. “I don’t believe we’ve met. I’m Valeria Moretti.”

His hand closed around mine, his grip firm and his skin noticeably warm. “The pleasure is mine, Ms. Moretti,” he said, his voice both smooth and serious. “I’ve heard a lot about you.”

I let out a small chuckle. “All good things, I hope?”

He gave a slight smile in return. “Depends who you ask. Some say you’re the jewel of your family. Others say you’re more trouble than you’re worth.”

His words were bold, but I refused to look away. “And you? What do you think?”

He paused for a moment, eyes studying me, and then said, “The truth is probably somewhere in the middle. I’d like to find out for myself.”

There was a tension in the air between us, something that pulled at me and made it impossible to look away. I felt a rush of adrenaline I hadn’t felt in years, knowing this could lead somewhere I might regret, but an undeniable part of me wanted to see where it would go.

As I turned to walk, I felt his hand rest lightly on my back, a simple gesture. There was nothing forceful in his touch, just a calm certainty.

A shiver ran through me, but I kept moving, aware of his presence with every step. That gentle control, the way he seemed to guide me without a word, was unexpected and left me quietly unsettled. Still, I let him steer, uncertain but drawn forward by curiosity.

We stepped out into the night air, city lights shining over Manhattan.

“Where to?” he asked, voice low.

I turned, a mix of excitement and fear in my chest. “Surprise me,” I said.

As we got into the waiting car, I understood I was crossing a line. But with Aldo’s eyes on me, I didn’t want to stop. For the first time in a long while, I felt free, and I wanted to see what would happen next.

## Chapter 2

Aldo

The black Audi moved quietly through Manhattan, neon lights flickering across the dashboard. The car, the driver, and the expensive hotel room all belonged to the FBI. I was just playing a part: the outsider, wealthy and interesting enough for the Morettis to let me in. Every piece of it was designed to sell that story.

Valeria sat next to me, legs crossed, watching the city blur by. There was a tension in the car that didn’t need words; her presence was strong even in silence. I caught the faint scent of jasmine, familiar, but edged with something sharper. She seemed both confident and unpredictable. I noticed the way she sat, the way she moved, as if she was always aware of the room and how much space she occupied.

I stuck to the role, every gesture and word considered. She was my way in, the person I needed to get close to for this to work. But there was something about her that kept me on edge, something that made me pay more attention than I should’ve. I couldn’t let myself forget why I was there, no matter how much she drew me in.

I couldn't afford that, not with Valeria.

This job was supposed to be straightforward. Get close, get information, help take down the Morettis. But with her, it was different. She wasn’t just another target.

I watched Valeria from the corner of my vision, careful not to let my attention linger too long. Up close, she made an impression; her features were sharp, her lips parted as if she were lost in thought. People liked to call her the mafia princess, but I could tell there was more to her than that. She carried herself with quiet confidence, never flinching or shrinking back, even when I touched her back. She seemed used to attention, maybe even expected it, but she never gave away control.

That was important. She wasn’t here for me; she was the reason I was here, my assignment. Every move mattered; she was my way into the Moretti family and everything connected to them. The badge in my pocket was a constant reminder: this was about the job, not about getting distracted by her presence.

There was an unpredictability to her, something simmering underneath the calm. She met my eyes directly back at the Plaza, no hesitation. Most people would have looked away or tried to soften the moment. Not her. She met the challenge.

That’s what set her apart. She was never going to be easy to read or control. It was clear she’d push back if I tried. Still, I had to stay focused. She was my entry point, nothing more.

Yet, I couldn’t help but wonder what was beneath that calm, how much of it was real. The pull was there, but I couldn’t let it cloud my judgment. Not with Valeria. She was important, and I couldn’t afford to forget it.

But damn, she was intoxicating.

“There’s a spot nearby,” I said, keeping my tone steady even if my mind was busy. “Quiet. We can talk.”

She turned, meeting my eyes with a small, unreadable smile. I couldn’t tell if it was real or for show. With Valeria Moretti, it was probably a bit of both. She always seemed a step ahead, and she knew I realized that.

City lights blurred past as we drove, and the air between us grew heavier. She shifted closer, fingers tapping quietly on her leg. There was an unmistakable tension. She seemed ready for something, and for once, I wasn’t sure if I was prepared.

“Lead the way, Mr. Cavalli,” she said, her voice calm but with an edge.

We stopped in front of a brownstone, the car engine fading to silence. Outside noise drifted back in: distant voices, a horn, and faint music from inside. I glanced at Valeria. She seemed comfortable, as if she belonged here. She understood this wasn’t just an ordinary bar.

We entered through an unmarked door, a guard outside giving us a quick look. My hand found the small of her back as we walked in, almost without thinking.

Inside, the design was simple and quiet: dark wood, leather, warm lighting. The kind of place where people talked in low voices and didn’t ask too many questions.

I led Valeria to a booth in the corner, keeping an eye on the room. Some habits stick, no matter where you are.

She looked around and nodded. “Impressive,” she said. “Didn’t know about this place.”

I signaled the waiter and ordered two glasses of Macallan, the thirty-year-old kind, no sense in settling for less. “I make it a habit to learn the hidden corners here,” I said, my voice carrying just enough hint of danger. “Especially the ones with the right sort of privacy.”

Valeria’s eyebrow lifted, interest flickering in her eyes. “And what sort would that be, Mr. Cavalli?”

I leaned in, lowering my voice. “The kind that values discretion, Ms. Moretti. Cities like this, secrets keep them running.”

Our drinks arrived. Valeria took a slow sip, her movements careful and practiced. Beneath the surface, I could sense something more, but I kept my focus.

“So,” I asked, glancing around, “what’s it like, growing up surrounded by all this?” I gestured toward the room. “I imagine there are advantages.”

Valeria’s expression shifted, just for a second. “Advantages?” she repeated, her tone reserved. “That depends. Some doors open, others close.”

I raised an eyebrow, keeping it light. “And the ones that close? That sounds…difficult.”

She gave a brief, humorless smile. “It can be. People have their assumptions. Living up to them isn’t always simple.”

I leaned back, watching her. “Must be a lot to manage.”

For a moment, something unreadable crossed her eyes. “It comes with the territory. Expectations, plans, they don’t stop.”

“From your family?” I asked, as if it were a casual question, though we both knew it wasn’t.

She paused, then nodded. “From everyone. But yes, especially from family.”

I kept that in mind. Every detail mattered. Valeria wasn’t just another guest here; she was my way into the Moretti family. This wasn’t just a conversation; it was an opportunity. The more I saw, the clearer it became that Valeria was more than just a piece in the game.

She had intelligence, sure, but also something deeper, resentment that didn’t come from money or comfort. It hinted at real fractures behind the Moretti family’s polished front. The kind of thing the FBI noticed, the kind I needed to get close to if I wanted to do my job.

This wasn’t just about getting her attention; it was about earning her trust, slowly, until she’d let me in. I’d done this work before, but Valeria was different. She wasn’t someone I could win over easily, and part of me respected that, even when I shouldn’t.

The job was getting complicated. She wasn’t the straightforward target I’d expected. Still, the task remained the same: get in, gather what I needed, and leave. No room for distractions, no matter how much she drew me in.

She looked at me, directly. “And what about you? What brings a man like Aldo Cavalli to New York? Wasn’t Chicago enough?”

I managed a small smile. “New York seemed like the right place for something new. Plenty of possibilities here.”

She didn’t look away. “And what possibilities are you after, Mr. Cavalli?”

The conversation hung between us, somewhere between challenge and interest. I found myself wanting to know more about her, even if that wasn’t part of the plan.

“The kind that changes things,” I said quietly. “The kind you can’t manage alone.”

Valeria’s lips parted, her breath quickening. “And what makes you think I’d want any sort of partnership with you?”

I reached out, my fingertips just brushing hers across the table. The touch caught us both off guard. I could see it in her eyes, that brief flash of surprise.

“Because, Ms. Moretti,” I said quietly, “I think you’re searching for something outside of what your family expects. And maybe you sense I could help you find it.”

She paused, studying me. Then, a small, careful smile appeared, measured, but impossible to ignore.

“You’re taking a risk, Mr. Cavalli,” she replied, her voice low.

I leaned in a bit, enough to show I wasn’t backing down. “Sometimes those risks pay off.”

The tension between us was impossible to miss. I was well aware of the stakes, but right then, I was willing to take the chance.

“Maybe we should talk somewhere private?” I suggested, my voice steady.

Valeria’s expression shifted, a mix of challenge and curiosity in her eyes. “Your move, Mr. Cavalli,” she said, making it clear the next step was mine.

## Chapter 1

The waiting room was crowded. Mia Eaton wasn’t sure where to sit. She didn’t really want to get into anyone else’s personal space, but she didn’t have much of a choice. The receptionist barked at her, “I said you can take a seat.”

Mia turned and smiled at her, having heard her the first time, but still pondering where to sit. Finally, she decided to take the chair between a large busted blonde and an older brunette who looked as nervous as Mia felt. It was a tight squeeze because the chairs were so close together. With her small build, it was easy to wedge her way in, but it was still uncomfortable. She sat with her legs squeezed together, her meager resume clutched tightly within the leather binder she’d borrowed from her neighbor, praying one of the girls sitting next to her was called back soon.

“Linda McKay!” a short woman with a severe haircut shouted from the door next to the receptionist. An attractive redhead sitting across the room stood up and walked to the door her head held high as if she had plenty of experience applying for secretarial positions and knew exactly what to expect. Mia sucked in air. She did not.

In fact, she’d never had any sort of secretarial job before at all. She’d dropped out of college after finishing her sophomore year to take care of her sick mother. She’d had to support both of them, too, and she’d done that by working as a cashier at a gas station near their home in a suburb of Chicago. But now that her mother had passed away, and Mia had sold everything in order to afford the first few months of rent on a small apartment, she knew it was now or never.

She had been on a few interviews but not for secretarial positions. Just a sales and a custodial position she almost hoped she didn’t get. She knew she wouldn’t be able to sell water to a man dying in the dessert, and she wouldn’t want to clean up after the residents in the nursing home either. No, as badly as she needed a job, she sort of hoped it wouldn’t be any of those.

Secretarial work seemed easy enough. She’d been a marketing major in college, before she’d been forced to drop out. She’d done well in her classes, so when she’d seen there was a secretarial opening at Whitaker and Whitaker Marketing Firm, she’d called right away. That was yesterday. They’d told her to be there at 3:00 today, and she’d arrived at 2:45. As many people as there were in the waiting room, she wondered how long it might take. Apparently, she hadn’t been the only one told to be there at that specific time.

It didn’t take long for Linda McKay to come back out. She didn’t look nearly as confident walking back this way as she had when she was headed in. A few seconds later, the severe woman was back. “Bridgette Duncan!” she yelled.

The girl a few chairs down from Mia stood. She was wearing a very short skirt, and the top three buttons of her blouse were unbuttoned. She had on heels that had to be at least six inches high and pencil thin.

She didn’t even make it over to the door before the woman looked her up and down and said, “No.”

Bridgette stood there for a second, as if she couldn’t quite believe her ears, but then she turned and slunk away. The woman shut the door, and Mia sucked in air, wondering what the woman done wrong. Had it been the outfit or something else?

Mia definitely wasn’t wearing an outfit like that, though her clothes were nothing to be proud of. The beige skirt had been her mother’s, and it was a size or two too big. Mia had safety pinned it earlier that morning when she’d left her apartment. It seemed to be holding up even though she’d spent a great deal of time at a coffeeshop trying to find other places to apply. The white button down shirt she wore was her own, but she’d had it for a few years, and it was a little stretched. Still, she thought she looked nice. She’d touched up her makeup and brushed out her long black hair before she rode up to the sixty-ninth floor on the elevator.

“Sandy Wilcox!” the woman shouted, the door hardly open this time.

The blonde next to Mia got up, giving her a small amount of room for a moment, but then another girl walked in, checked with reception, and came to sit next to Mia, causing her to tense up again.

A few people were staring at their phones, but Mia was too nervous to let go of her binder. Her bag was by her feet, and all she could think about was the worn spot on the leather toward the zipper. She almost didn’t realize her name was being called until the woman said it again. “Hello? Mia Eaton? Anyone?”

“So sorry,” Mia said, shaking her head as she grabbed her belongings and stood, almost dropping her binder. She pulled her purse over her arm and tucked the binder under her arm and approached the door, certain she was about to be sent out the door like that poor woman in the stilettos.

Severe Haircut looked her up and down, huffed, and gestured for her to follow behind.

Mia took a deep breath and went through the door, praying she hadn’t already ruined her chances before she even got to the interview.

## Chapter 2

“My name is Veronica Smithers. I’m Mr. Whitaker’s personal assistant. I do most everything for him. It is important that whomever fills this position realizes that it isn’t just about answering phones and sending correspondence. You may be asked to perform any sort of task throughout the day, some you could easily think of, such as making coffee or running to the nearest coffeeshop. Others may never cross your mind until the question is raised.” Veronica turned and looked at her, and Mia nodded, feeling pricks of ice radiate through her veins as she attempted to decipher what that might mean.

They were walking through a vast space of cubicles and offices with people working in groups, pairs, and all alone, but Mia was struggling to keep up with Veronica and hardly had a chance to look around her. Eventually, they reached a small office, and Veronica walked in, stepping behind an organized desk with a huge stack of papers on it. She gestured for Mia to take a seat, which she did, and that’s when she realized the papers were all resumes.

Veronica thrust her hand foreword, clearly wanting something. Still stunned by the enormous stack of applicants, Mia was confused. She looked at Veronica’s open palm and then up to her eyes. “Resume?” the woman said, practically rolling her eyes at her.

“Of course. I apologize. I’m a little nervous.” Mia fumbled for the zipper on the side of her leather portfolio case. It snagged, stuck, and nearly broke. She took a deep breath, tried to smile, and tried again, catching her nail and ripping it. The sting wasn’t as bad as the embarrassment. Veronica was growing impatient.

The third try was the charm; she managed to get her portfolio open and work the single page resume out, handing it over with what she hoped was a confident smile. Compared to the page on the top of the stack, it looked as if Mia had never worked before. The other girl’s resume was nearly full and looked well-organized. Mia had put hers together the afternoon before in the library and printed it for ten cents on the high quality library copy paper.

It only took Veronica a moment to look over the resume. She sat it aside. “What are your strengths?”

“Well, I, uh… love marketing,” Mia began, smiling and hoping she could get her nerves under control. “I studied it in college. I’m a hard worker. I’m always pleasant. Easy to get along with.”

“Uh huh. And other than your complete lack of any work experience even remotely related to the secretarial field, what are your weaknesses?”

Doing her best to disregard the low blow, Mia kept her smile in place. “I am very trusting, which is sometimes seen as gullible,” she admitted. “I do have a bit of a problem with distractions from time to time, though it’s nothing I can’t work through.” She looked Veronica in the eyes and knew there was no way she was getting this job. Mia blew out a long breath. “But… as you mentioned, I’ve never done secretarial work before. I can type fast and accurately. I’m very friendly on the phone, and I’m willing to learn.”

“I take it you’d finished answering my question about your weaknesses before that last part.”

Veronica looked annoyed that Mia had strayed from her initial question. “Yes, ma’am. I apologize.”

“Uh huh,” the woman said, still scowling. Her eyes flickered down the resume again, but then she looked back at Mia, seeming to study her. “If you were to get the position, when could you start?”

“Right away,” Mia said with a confident nod. “I just moved here, so I don’t have a job yet—”

Veronica didn’t care. “And you understand that the salary is base plus bonuses you may earn for taking on additional tasks and for performance that Mr. Whitaker deems above and beyond?”

“Yes, Ms. Smithers,” she said with a nod. The salary, even with no bonuses, was enough for her to pay her rent, as well as her other bills, and still put some money back each month.

Ms. Smithers cleared her throat and picked up the telephone next to her elbow. She punched the top number and waited a second. Mia wasn’t sure what to do. It seemed odd she’d be calling someone in the middle of her interview.

Though she couldn’t make out what was being said, it was clear a male’s voice was speaking on the other end of the phone. It was a deep tenor, raspy, gravelly. Mia crossed her legs and tried not to twist her long black hair around her finger.

“Yes. Thank you,” Veronica said and hung up the phone. “You may go.”

Mia was shocked at such a quick dismissal. Granted, she’d seen the other women coming and going so quickly, she’d been shocked Veronica had kept her this long.

“Please, Ms. Smithers, if you give me a chance—”

“You. May. Go!”

“Yes, ma’am.” Realizing there was nothing else she could do, Mia gathered her bag and tucked her portfolio under her arm, half wishing she could ask for her resume back so she wouldn’t have to waste another dime getting a new one for her next interview. Clearly, this one would wither away in that immense stack of papers for a few days before it died a horrible death in the shredder. “Thank you for your time.”

Veronica only nodded, and Mia got up, headed back the way she came. The only problem was, she had no idea how she got there. Since Veronica had not followed her out, she didn’t know which direction to turn. She went down a hall, thinking maybe it was that way, but that ended up at a dead end. She turned back around and went the other direction, thinking she’d just ask someone when she ran right into a solid wall of muscle.

“Are you lost?”

Mia looked up into bright blue eyes, and all the breath left her lungs as she stammered for an answer. If she wasn’t lost before, she was now.

## Chapter 3

“Can I help you?”

Mia knew she was staring, that the man with the gorgeous blue eyes was speaking to her, that she’d looked up after the collision but hadn’t backed away, so the foot or so between them was due to him retreating while she still hadn’t found her voice or her ability to move.

“Are you lost?”

“Uh… yeah,” she finally managed, snapping out of it. She took a giant step backward and ran her hand through her hair. It happened to be the hand her purse was swung over, so when she did that, it swung back and forth violently before falling off of her shoulder. She caught it on her wrist momentarily, but then it fell to the floor. “Dang it!”

“Let me get that for you,” he said, stooping to get it, but by then, Mia had already gone to retrieve it herself. She hit her head on his shoulder hard. “Oh, God. Are you okay?”

Wincing, Mia rubbed her head. How strong was this man that hitting her head on his shoulder was like ramming her head into a brick wall? “I’m fine.”

He picked up her bag, and the two of them stood, though Mia could tell he was being careful to give her plenty of space. “Here you go.”

“Thank you.” She took the bag and slung it back over her shoulder, trying not to roll her eyes at how stupid she must look. It was probably a good thing that she wasn’t going to be getting a job here or else she might literally run into this guy again. Or do something else stupid in front of him. “Can you tell me how to get out?”

He smirked at her, as if he could tell just how badly she wanted to get away. “I’ll show you. It can be a little tricky.”

“Thanks.” She wondered if any of the other candidates had gotten lost and assumed they hadn’t.

Following him back the way she’d come, she couldn’t help but notice how nice he looked from the back. She had to pull her eyes away from his perfectly sculpted bottom when they entered the area where so many other workers were sitting. She didn’t want to seem like a scumbag, but then, she’d never seen a man like this one before—not in real life—not that she could remember.

“Did you apply for a position here?” he asked as they were walking along, stopping to wait for her.

“I did,” Mia admitted, coming even with his shoulder. He was at least a foot taller than her. “But I’m pretty sure I didn’t get it.”

“Oh? Why is that?” he asked, looking disappointed. Mia figured he was just being overly polite.

She shrugged. “The interview only took about twenty seconds. I’m probably not even qualified.”

They rounded another corner, and she could see the exit now. “What position did you apply for?”

“It’s a secretarial position,” she said, stopping and looking down at her shoes. It was almost impossible to continue to look into his eyes without feeling drained.

“Anyone can do that,” he said. “What makes you think you’re not qualified?”

“I don’t know. I’ve never done it before.”

“What have you done before?”

Something about the way he asked the question made her wonder if he was still talking about work. His cologne was spicy, a hint of sandalwood blending with cedar, and she had a feeling there was a note in his masculine scent that was all him. Mia bit her bottom lip and tried to get her head together. “Uh… nothing.”

“Nothing?” He lifted a dark eyebrow. Her answer seemed to intrigue him for reasons she couldn’t let herself contemplate.

“Not really. I worked as a cashier at a gas station while I took care of my mom.”

“Was she ill?” His tone changed to something less suggestive and more concerned.

Mia nodded. Her mother had been dead for almost six months, but she still missed her terribly. “She passed away, so I moved to the big city.”

“I’m so sorry for your loss.”

He seemed to sincerely mean that, and Mia felt a tear coming to her eye. So many people said it but it was just something one said off the cuff, as if they didn’t really feel it. She could tell by his eyes that he did. “Thank you.”

A heavy silence fell over them. Mia struggled for something else to say, but there wasn’t any more. He’d shown her to the exit; she wasn’t getting this job anyway. She’d never see him again.

He seemed at a loss for words as well, which she guessed was out of character for him. “Well, I hope you get the job,” he said with a small smile, and she almost thought he meant it.

“I appreciate that. Thank you. And thanks for showing me out.” She gestured toward the door with a thumb over her shoulder.

“You bet. Maybe I’ll see you around…?”

He was waiting for her name. This gorgeous, sexy man with beautiful blue eyes and the kind of grin that morphed between boy-next-door and spank you till you can’t breathe wanted to know her name.

The only problem was… she couldn’t remember it.

“I’m sorry—I didn’t catch your name,” he said, prompting her.

Too bad she hadn’t grabbed that copy of her resume. It was probably on there. “My… uh….” Oh, yeah—duh—that was it. “Mia. My name is Mia.”

That grin was back, the mischievous crooked one. “Mia?”

“Yes.”

He stuck out his right hand, and she stared at it for a moment, wondering what sorts of things it was capable of before she slipped her tiny palm inside. His touch was light at first, but then firm and commanding as he shook her hand and electric pulses shot up her arm. “I’m Beau.”

“Beau.” As in beautiful, she thought to herself. “It’s nice to meet you, too.”

“Take care, Mia.”

She smiled and then turned to go, almost smacking into the doorway but catching herself and not daring to turn and look at him again to see if he’d noticed. He had to have—she could practically feel his eyes on the back of her.

Back in the waiting room, she ignored the sighs from everyone else who likely assumed she’d been interviewing that whole time, rather than just wandering aimlessly. She couldn’t help but smile, though. Even if she never saw Beau again, the encounter had been memorable. Maybe he’d get his wish, and she would come to work there. Then what? She didn’t know, but she was looking forward to finding out.

## Chapter 4

Walking into his brother’s office, Beau Whitaker waited for Sam to get off of the phone before he said anything at all. When Sam finally hung up and looked up at him, Beau wasn’t even sure where to begin.

He wanted to seem nonchalant, but the girl he’d met in the hallway—Mia—was so beautiful, so intriguing, he wanted to make sure Sam was aware that Beau wouldn’t mind it if he hired her as his new secretary. In fact, if he had any say in it at all, Mia already had the job.

“What’s up, little brother?” Sam asked, making a note on a sticky before attaching it to a file and moving it across his desk. “Need something?”

Beau snickered. He didn’t come into Sam’s office often, unless he needed something. There was usually no need to. Sam handled new accounts; Beau handled existing accounts. If they ever needed to meet, their offices had an adjoining conference room where they could discuss whatever they needed to. The view out the floor to ceiling windows of downtown Chicago was breathtaking, but Beau had a similar view out his own window. So… the fact that he was standing there at all was telling.

“I hear you’re looking for a new secretary,” he finally said, running his fingers along the edge of Sam’s large, finely finished mahogany desk.

“I don’t have a choice,” Sam replied, clicking his pen a few times as he leaned back in his chair. “Since Bridgette quit, I have to have someone around here to answer the phones.”

Beau snickered. They both knew Bridgette’s jobs had been plentiful, but answering the phones was rarely one of the duties Sam tasked her with. “Hazards of dating a co-worker, I guess. You break up with her, she’s gotta go.”

“I’d hardly say we were dating,” Sam argued, sweeping his shaggy dark bangs out of his eye. The brothers looked very similar—same build, same dark hair, but Sam was slightly shorter, a little broader in the shoulders, and his eyes were a jade green while Beaus were the same shade that their mother’s had been.

“True. That’s hardly what I’d call it either, but I was trying to be polite, I guess.”

Sam gestured with his arms wide. “For whose benefit?”

Knowing he was wasting his breath in further explanation, Beau sank down on the edge of one of the two leather upholstered chairs across from his brother’s desk. “Any prospects?”

“A ton,” Sam said, sighing as if he was the one who had to dig through the stack of applicants or even do any of the interviews. “I’ve been keeping an eye on things.”

“How?”

Sam picked up a tablet off of his desk, flipped it on, and handed it over.

Veronica’s office came into view. It was clear she was wearing a lapel pen that allowed Sam to drop in any time. Across from his assistant, Beau could see a beautiful woman with long, blonde hair sat across from her. It was on mute, but it would’ve been easy for Beau to listen to the interview if he wanted to. “So… what’s your method here?” He offered the iPad back to his brother.

Sam took it and sat it down on his desk in front of him, only glancing at it briefly. “If it’s a girl Veronica thinks I might be interested in, she calls me, I drop in, check her out, and let Veronica know.”

“How many girls have you been interested in?”

Shrugging, Sam said, “I don’t know. Five or six.”

“Do you know their names?”

Now, Sam knew something was up. “Why do you want to know?”

Beau couldn’t keep the smirk off of his face. “I may have ran into one of your potential candidates in the hall, and I was hoping… maybe you’d consider hiring her.”

Leaning forward in his seat, Sam stared at Beau for a few moments before he said, “Considering the types of services I ask my secretary to perform, why would you want me to hire a woman you’re obviously interested in?”

It was a good question. “I guess… I just want to see her again.”

“You want her phone number?”

Beau chuckled. “No.” He ran a hand through his hair. He felt ridiculous. Why not just call Mia himself. He pulled himself up out of the chair. “Never mind.”

“What? Why?” Sam asked, his hands stretched out again. “You like her or not? Since when are you so shy?”

“I’m not.” He walked toward the door. “I’m not. I just… wanted to know what you thought, I guess.”

Sam still had a smirk on his face. “What’s her name?”

Beau didn’t even want to tell him. “It’s… uh… Mia.”

Sam’s countenance changed completely as he studied Beau’s face for a moment. Then, tapping his pen against his chin a few times, he asked, “Long, black hair? Petite—unassuming? Maybe a little lost? Potentially innocent in every way?”

Swallowing hard at the objectivity his brother had just used to describe the sweet, beautiful girl he’d found wandering the hallways, Beau blew out a deep breath. “Yeah, that’s her.”

A rich chuckle emanated from Sam’s throat. “Funny. When I saw her, I thought she looked like the sort of girl you’d be excited about.”

Shaking his head, Beau turned back toward the door. Maybe he should go get Mia’s number from Veronica. It would be stupid and potentially dangerous for him to let Mia work for Sam anyway. He definitely did know what his older brother, by mere minutes, asked his secretaries to do, and little of it was secretarial.

“She’s one of my five or six,” Sam shouted as Beau walked halfway out the door. “You still want me to hire her? Maybe we can ask her to handle secretarial services for both of us.”

Hearing what Sam wasn’t saying, Beau hesitated. He rarely dated women like Mia. His brother had been right about her unassuming personality appealing to him, but he dated rich, elite women, aspiring models, daughters of well-respect businessmen. Not girls who just relocated to the city and had safety pins holding their skirts up.

But he’d liked her immediately. If she worked here, he wouldn’t necessarily have to date her to see her. If she was the sort of girl that would bend to Sam’s expectations, he might not have to date her to receive her services either.

Realizing his inner thoughts reflected he was a bit more like his brother than he was willing to admit, Beau found himself nodding. “Yeah, I want you to hire her.”

## Chapter 1

[Tessa]

The bus lurches to a stop, and I'm the first one out, eager to stretch my legs after the long journey. As I step onto the snow-covered ground, my breath catches in my throat. The Colorado Rockies loom before me, majestic and intimidating, their snow-capped peaks seeming to touch the cloudless blue sky.

"Holy shit," I whisper, drinking in the view. The mountains are a challenge—a dare—and my heart races with anticipation. This is what I've been training for.

"Tessa! Wait up!" Sam's voice calls from behind me. I turn to see my best friend stumbling off the bus, her arms full of gear.

"Sorry," I say, reaching out to steady her. "I got a little awestruck."

Sam grins, her cheeks already flushed from the cold. "Can't blame you. These mountains are something else."

We make our way to the lodge, our boots crunching in the fresh snow. The air is crisp and clean, filled with the scent of pine. It's invigorating, and I feel my spirits lifting with each breath.

"So," Sam says, bumping my shoulder. "You ready to show these trust fund babies how it's done?"

I laugh, but there's an edge to it. "You know it. They may have the fancy gear, but we've got heart."

And determination, I add silently. And the need to prove ourselves.

The lodge is a bustle of activity, skiers and organizers milling about. I scan the crowd, half-expecting to see a familiar face—one I'm not quite ready to confront. But he's not here. Not yet.

We check in and head to our room. It's small but cozy, with two twin beds and a window overlooking the slopes. I drop my bags and immediately start unpacking, my movements quick and efficient.

"Whoa, slow down there, speed racer," Sam jokes, flopping onto her bed. "The slopes aren't going anywhere."

I ignore her, focusing on laying out my gear. My hands move over each piece with practiced ease—goggles, gloves, thermal layers. Everything has its place, everything serves a purpose. Control what you can control, my dad always says.

"Earth to Tessa," Sam says, waving a hand in front of my face. "You okay? You seem a little... intense."

I pause, realizing I've been meticulously arranging and rearranging my ski poles for the last five minutes. "Yeah, I'm fine," I say, not meeting her eyes. "Just want to make sure everything's perfect."

Sam sits up, her expression softening. "Is this about the race, or is it about him?"

My hands still. "I don't know what you're talking about."

"Oh, come on," Sam says, rolling her eyes. "Mr. Tall, Dark, and Broody? The guy who's had you all wound up for years? Ring any bells?"

I feel my cheeks heat up, and it's not from the altitude. "Max has nothing to do with this," I say, my voice sharper than I intend. "I'm here to ski. That's all."

Sam holds up her hands in surrender. "Okay, okay. Just... don't let him get in your head, alright? You're a kickass skier, Tess. You don't need to prove anything to anyone."

I nod, grateful for her support even as doubt gnaws at me. Because the truth is, I do need to prove something. To myself, to the skiing world, and yes, to Max Donovan.

As Sam heads to the bathroom to freshen up, I turn my attention to my most prized possession—my skis. They're not the newest model or the most expensive brand, but they're mine. I've poured countless hours and every spare penny into maintaining them, and they've never let me down.

I run my fingers along the edges, checking for any nicks or imperfections. The familiar routine soothes me, grounding me in the present. But as I work, my mind drifts back to the last time I saw Max, three years ago at another charity event.

The memory hits me with startling clarity. I can still feel the biting cold of that day, see the disapproval in Max's green eyes as he looked down at me—literally and figuratively.

"You're going to get yourself killed skiing like that," he had said, his voice as icy as the slopes around us. "It's reckless and unprofessional."

I remember the fury that had coursed through me, hot enough to melt the snow at my feet. "And you're going to bore yourself to death skiing like a robot," I had shot back. "Some of us actually enjoy the sport, you know."

His jaw had clenched, a muscle ticking in his cheek. "Enjoyment doesn't win races or keep you safe. Discipline does."

"Right, because you're such an expert on winning these days," I had sneered, immediately regretting the words as hurt flashed in his eyes. But I was too angry, too proud to take them back.

Max had straightened, his expression hardening into a mask of indifference. "Good luck in the race, Ms. Greene," he had said coldly. "Try not to crash and burn." And then he had walked away, leaving me fuming in the snow.

I shake my head, dispelling the memory. My hands have stilled on my skis, and I realize I've been gripping them so tightly, my knuckles have turned white.

"Get it together, Tessa," I mutter to myself. "He's just another competitor. Nothing more."

But even as I say the words, I know they're a lie. Max Donovan has never been just another competitor to me. He's been my rival, my inspiration, my frustration, and sometimes, in the quietest corners of my mind, something else entirely.

I finish my equipment check just as Sam emerges from the bathroom. "All set?" she asks, eyeing my meticulously arranged gear.

I nod, forcing a smile. "Ready as I'll ever be."

We head down to the welcome dinner, the lodge buzzing with excitement. As we enter the dining hall, my eyes automatically scan the crowd. I tell myself I'm just getting a feel for the competition, but deep down, I know who I'm looking for.

And then I see him.

Max is standing near the fireplace, deep in conversation with one of the event organizers. He looks good—too good. His dark hair is slightly tousled, like he's just taken off his beanie, and his green eyes are intense as he listens to whatever the organizer is saying.

As if sensing my gaze, Max looks up. Our eyes lock across the room, and for a moment, everything else fades away. There's surprise in his expression, then something else—something that makes my heart stutter in my chest.

And then Sam is pulling me towards the buffet, breaking the connection. "Come on," she says, oblivious to the moment I've just had. "Let's fuel up. You've got some ass to kick tomorrow."

I let her lead me away, but I can feel Max's eyes on me as we go. It's going to be a long week, I think, my determination warring with a flutter of anticipation in my stomach.

And I'm ready to see what happens.

## Chapter 2

[Max]

I step out of the private car, sunglasses firmly in place, and plaster on my best camera-ready smile. The crisp mountain air hits me, carrying with it the scent of pine and snow. For a moment, just a fleeting second, I'm transported back to my competition days. The thrill, the anticipation, the rush of adrenaline before a big race.

Then reality crashes back. I'm not here to compete. Not anymore.

"Max! Over here!" 

"Mr. Donovan, can we get a statement?"

"Max, how does it feel to be back on the slopes?"

The barrage of questions and camera flashes assault me, and I fall back on years of media training. Smile, wave, give them just enough to keep them happy without revealing anything real.

"It's great to be here," I say, my voice carrying easily over the clamor. "I'm looking forward to supporting this fantastic cause and seeing some world-class skiing."

As I make my way through the crowd, signing autographs and posing for selfies, I can't help but scan the faces around me. I tell myself I'm just getting a feel for the event, but deep down, I know who I'm looking for. Who I'm dreading—and maybe hoping—to see.

Tessa Greene.

The last time I saw her, we'd had a heated argument that left a bitter taste in my mouth. Her words still echo in my mind: "Right, because you're such an expert on winning these days." The memory stings, a sharp reminder of everything I've lost.

I push the thought away as I spot James Montgomery making his way towards me. James, the CEO of the company that sponsors me, is all smiles and handshakes as he approaches.

"Max! Glad you made it," he says, clapping me on the shoulder. "How was the drive up?"

"Long," I admit, allowing a small, genuine smile. "But the views made up for it. These mountains never get old."

James nods, his eyes gleaming with barely contained excitement. "Wait until you see the course they've set up. It's going to be one hell of a race."

The mention of the race sends a pang through my chest, a mixture of longing and frustration that I quickly suppress. "I'm sure it will be," I say, keeping my tone neutral. "When's the meeting with the organizers?"

"Right now, actually," James says, checking his watch. "Shall we?"

I nod, grateful for the distraction. As we make our way to the lodge, I can't help but notice the way other skiers and guests turn to stare. Some with admiration, others with pity. I'm not sure which is worse.

Inside, the lodge is a hive of activity. Skiers, organizers, and media personnel buzz around, their excitement palpable. The smell of coffee and pine mingles in the air, and for a moment, I'm hit with a wave of nostalgia so strong, it almost knocks me off my feet.

"You okay?" James asks, noticing my hesitation.

I nod, forcing myself back to the present. "Yeah, just... taking it all in."

The meeting room is mercifully quiet compared to the lobby. A group of event organizers is already seated around a large oak table, their faces lighting up as James and I enter.

"Mr. Donovan, it's an honor to have you here," one of them, a middle-aged woman with a no-nonsense haircut, says as she stands to shake my hand. "I'm Sarah Winters, head of the organizing committee."

"Please, call me Max," I say, shaking her hand firmly. "It's great to be here. You've put together quite an event."

As we take our seats, Sarah launches into a detailed explanation of the event schedule, the charity beneficiaries, and the course layout. I listen attentively, asking questions and offering suggestions where appropriate. This is familiar territory—the business side of skiing that I've immersed myself in since my injury.

But as Sarah describes the racecourse, I feel a familiar itch in my palms, a restlessness in my legs. The urge to strap on my skis and tackle the mountain myself is almost overwhelming.

"And of course, we're thrilled to have you judge the freestyle competition," Sarah says, snapping me back to attention. "Your expertise will be invaluable."

I nod, pushing down the twinge of regret. "I'm looking forward to it. We've got some real talent in the lineup this year."

"Speaking of talent," James cuts in, leaning forward with a gleam in his eye. "Any standouts you've got your eye on, Max? We're always on the lookout for the next big star."

The question catches me off guard, and unbidden, an image of Tessa flashes through my mind—her fierce determination, the way she attacked the slopes with a reckless abandon that both terrified and exhilarated me.

"It's... too early to say," I hedge, aware of the expectant looks around the table. "I'll need to see them on the slopes first."

James nods, but I can see the disappointment in his eyes. He's been pushing me to find new talent, to prove my worth beyond my own skiing career. It's a pressure I'm not sure I'm ready to handle.

The meeting wraps up shortly after, and I find myself being ushered from one commitment to another. Photo ops, interviews, meet-and-greets with sponsors. By the time I finally make it to my suite, I'm exhausted, my public persona slipping away like snow melting in the sun.

The suite is luxurious, with floor-to-ceiling windows offering a breathtaking view of the mountains. But my eyes are drawn to the familiar leather case sitting on the dresser. Inside, I know, are my old trophies—a request from the event organizers for a display in the lodge.

With a sigh, I open the case. The gold and silver gleam in the fading light, each one a memory of triumph, of pushing myself to the limit and coming out on top. I pick up the largest one, from my last world championship before the injury.

The weight of it in my hands brings back a flood of memories: the roar of the crowd, the bite of cold air on my face as I flew down the slope, the indescribable feeling of knowing, even before I crossed the finish line, that I'd won.

And then, sharp and vivid, the memory of my last race. The sickening crack as my ski caught, the world spinning out of control, the blinding pain. The long months of surgeries and rehab, only to be told I'd never compete again.

I set the trophy down harder than necessary, turning away from the case. My eyes land on the window, on the mountains beyond. Somewhere out there, Tessa Greene is preparing for tomorrow's race. Probably pushing herself to the limit, taking risks that make my heart race just thinking about them.

Part of me wants to find her, to warn her about the dangers of skiing the way she does. But I know how that conversation would go. She'd accuse me of being a has-been, of trying to hold her back out of jealousy or bitterness.

And maybe she'd be right.

A knock at the door startles me out of my thoughts. "Mr. Donovan?" a voice calls. "Your presence is requested at the welcome dinner."

I close my eyes, taking a deep breath. Time to put the mask back on. "I'll be right there," I call back, already reaching for my jacket.

As I head for the door, I catch a glimpse of myself in the mirror. I look every inch the successful ex-athlete turned businessman. But in my eyes, I can see the shadow of doubt, the longing for what I've lost.

I straighten my shoulders, fixing my expression into one of confident ease. It's going to be a long week, I think, as I step out into the hallway. But as I make my way to the elevator, a small part of me can't help but look forward to seeing Tessa again, to feeling that spark of challenge she always ignites in me.
